questions.question: Compare how PON and the lift-and-splat method move image features toward BEV, naming the first operation in each.

The lift-and-splat method first lifts each image into a per-pixel depth frustum, then splats all frustums into the BEV grid (slide 42). questions.question: Describe how the RPN defines anchors and how it labels them as foreground or background during training, according to this course's deck.

Per this course's deck, an anchor is labeled foreground if its IoU with a ground-truth object exceeds 0.5, and background if it has no overlap or less than 0.1 IoU with any ground-truth object; anchors in between are excluded from the training mini-batch.

questions.question: Describe the overall pipeline of the Vision Transformer, from raw image input to the final classification output.
questions.answerText: ViT first splits the image into fixed-size patches and linearly embeds each patch using a Conv2d layer with kernel_size and stride equal to the patch size. A learnable class token is prepended to this sequence of patch embeddings, and a learnable position embedding (covering all N patches plus the class token) is added to inject positional information, since self-attention is otherwise permutation-invariant. The resulting sequence is processed through a standard Transformer encoder with alternating pre-normed MSA and MLP blocks plus residual connections, and the final output state of the class token is passed to a classifier head to produce the prediction.

COCO stores absolute top-left x, top-left y, width, and height in pixels inside a single JSON file. YOLO stores normalized [0,1] center x, center y, width, and height in per-image TXT files. A practical pitfall when converting between these is mixing inclusive versus exclusive box coordinate conventions, which can slightly change computed IoU, particularly for small objects.

questions.question: Describe the structure and purpose of a ResNet bottleneck block.

This structure makes the expensive 3x3 convolution cheaper by having it operate on fewer channels, while the residual add still provides the gradient-flow benefits of skip connections.

This is framed as a tradeoff because moving toward higher levels (like Level D or E) increases the system's learning capacity and flexibility but can reduce how easily the system's behavior can be verified, tested, or certified. Conversely, staying at a lower level like Level A preserves verifiability through a classic planner but may limit how much the system can learn and adapt. The challenge is thus to find a balance point rather than maximizing either property alone.

questions.question: Explain why the anchor head uses 6 anchors per location and what the 7 box values per anchor represent before decoding.

Each anchor's 7 box values are residuals relative to that anchor: normalized offsets for x, y, and z, log-ratio size changes for length, width, and height, and a heading difference. The residuals are decoded into a metric box only after training, as covered in the next topic.

questions.question: Explain the central conceptual shift DETR makes relative to prior object detectors, and summarize its high-level architecture.
questions.answerText: DETR reframes object detection as a direct set prediction problem rather than relying on dense anchors with NMS post-processing. It uses a set-based global loss built on bipartite matching to force unique one-to-one predictions. Architecturally, an image passes through a CNN backbone, then a Transformer encoder that lets image tokens exchange global context, then a decoder where a fixed set of learned object queries cross-attend to the encoder output, and finally classification and box heads produce the set of detections.

questions.question: Describe the inference path from dense head outputs to final detections, including the score step and why NMS is applied.
questions.answerText: The head outputs 321,408 anchors with class logits, box residuals, and direction logits. Inference applies a sigmoid to the class logits and takes the maximum class score per anchor, decodes residuals into boxes of the form [x, y, z, l, w, h, theta], and runs class-agnostic or multi-class NMS. The final output is pred_boxes, pred_scores, and pred_labels. NMS is needed because dense anchors produce many overlapping boxes around one object.

questions.question: Describe how the final predicted distance for a box side is computed from its DFL bin distribution, including the role of softmax.

questions.question: Describe how CSPNet's partitioning strategy works and why it is described as achieving a richer gradient combination with less computation.
questions.answerText: CSPNet partitions the base layer's feature map into two parts: one part flows through a stack of layers (such as the dense/residual blocks) and the other is passed through more directly, and the two paths are merged through a cross-stage hierarchy. By splitting the computation this way, CSPNet avoids redundant gradient information flowing through the entire network while still allowing diverse gradient paths, which reduces computation relative to processing the full feature map through every layer while the richer gradient combination improves training.

questions.question: Compute NDS for mAP = 0.5 and true-positive errors 0.30, 0.25, 0.40, 0.30, and 0.20. Then explain how a model that outputs no velocity would change the result.
questions.answerText: NDS = (5 x 0.5 + 3.55) / 10 = 0.605. A model that outputs no velocity has its velocity error set to the worst value, so the velocity error term contributes zero to the sum. That term carries weight 1/10 in NDS, so the score falls relative to mAP. The slide says such a model is capped well below its mAP.

questions.question: A classmate argues that solving BEV fusion and multi-sensor fusion around 2020 effectively finished the autonomy problem. Using the timeline, explain why this reasoning is flawed.
questions.answerText: The timeline explicitly documents two further eras after 2020: end-to-end policies and large multimodal models in 2024, and world models, physical AI, and agentic data engines in 2025-2026. The existence of these later, distinct bottlenecks shows that solving BEV and multi-sensor fusion did not end the field's open problems; it only shifted the dominant challenge forward.

questions.question: Explain the trade-off between pillars and voxels for a LiDAR detector, using the slide's pros and cons.
questions.answerText: Pillars collapse height into one column per cell, which allows pure 2D CNNs and is fast, but they lose fine height structure. Voxels keep height, but dense 3D convolution has cubic memory growth, so they need sparse convolution. The slides frame this as speed and simplicity against height detail and sparse-kernel cost.
